attacks.claim: External processor calls run after the DB transaction commits and retry for up to 7 days, but the identifiers they need (Stripe customer ID, Customer.io ID, Zendesk user ID, Amplitude ID, Apple refresh token) live in rows the transaction deletes. `deleted_accounts` keeps only user IDs and dates. The plan does not say where these IDs and tokens persist for the retries, nor how a crash between commit and enqueue is handled. Apple's `/auth/revoke` needs the stored refresh token.
attacks.evidence: "each account is one DB transaction across `users` and the 23 tables" ... "After the DB transaction commits: ... Sign in with Apple users: `POST /auth/revoke` for their refresh token" ... "`deleted_accounts` keeps only purged user IDs and dates (no PII)"

attacks.claim: The Art. 17 completeness guarantee is overstated. The CI check only catches columns named `user_id` or `*_user_id`, so tables using `author_id`, `owner_id`, `sender_id`, polymorphic references, or file attachments are missed. Non-DB stores are also unaddressed: object storage for uploads and the emailed export ZIPs, push tokens, and the transactional email provider. The 'no other system' claim rests on one inventory doc, with no test backing it.
attacks.evidence: "lists every table with a `user_id` or `*_user_id` column" ... "No other system holds user-level data beyond the processors below (data inventory DPI-2026"

attacks.claim: The worst-case timeline of 14 + 7 days assumes each processor deletes as soon as the API call is accepted. Processor-side completion is not verified, and some deletion APIs (Amplitude's, for example) are asynchronous or delayed. The dashboard and the '100% within 21 days' metric appear to measure call acceptance, not actual erasure, so the one-month claim is unproven.
attacks.evidence: "Worst-case (14 + 7 days) stays inside the one-month Art. 17 deadline." ... "100% of purges complete within 21 days of confirmation (dashboard)."

attacks.claim: An export requested just before the purge may still be queued or generating when the purge runs. The plan does not say whether it is delivered, fails, or leaves a ZIP in storage with no cleanup. The plan promises delivery 'after you confirm' but does not define behaviour past day 14.
attacks.evidence: "An export requested here is still delivered after you confirm deletion."

attacks.claim: Purge is irreversible, yet only the first batch is dry-run. There is no stated pause switch for the purge job, which explicitly ignores the feature flag, if a registry bug (wrong delete vs nullify) is found after day 14.
attacks.evidence: "the purge job ignores the flag" ... "The first real purge batch ... runs in dry-run mode first"

attacks.claim: The 'real owner has 14 days' protection assumes the account email is unchanged. An attacker with the password could change the email first, or the plan does not say it notifies the old address, so the confirmation would go to the attacker. The per-email rate limit also lets a third party burn the victim's 3/day quota and spam them with deletion emails.
attacks.evidence: "The confirmation email gives the real owner 14 days to cancel even if their password was used." ... "3/day per email address"

attacks.claim: 'Keep my account' restores 'exactly as it was', but a Stripe subscription set to cancel at period end may already have lapsed within the 14 days. Unsetting the flag then cannot restore it.
attacks.evidence: "restores the account exactly as it was" ... ""Keep my account" unsets it."

attacks.claim: The schedule has no slack. The 3-week build covers 3 clients, a web page, a purge job, 5 processor integrations, a dashboard, a restore drill, and accessibility testing. Staff soak, 100% rollout and App Store resubmission all fall in week 3, and App Review turnaround is not accounted for, though all iOS releases are blocked.
attacks.evidence: "Week 3: staff accounts (60) first, then 100%, then App Store resubmission the same week."

attacks.claim: Backups (35 days) outlive the one-month erasure window, and logs and Sentry keep 30 days. The plan relies on a restore-reapply runbook rather than telling users. It does not say that §7 of the privacy policy discloses the backup retention.
attacks.evidence: "Postgres snapshots roll off after 35 days and are not edited."
